title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6715 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

For now the signal points the other way: diesel exports are falling and November tracking is weaker. The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts. When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET). Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on). As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Could the internet go dark?
body: Chimpanzees can choose the right tool for a task and even modify it in advance; crows drop stones into water to raise its level and reach floating food; and octopuses can unscrew jars to get to what's inside. That is called causal reasoning, something humans are particularly good at, although it can sometimes lead us down the wrong path. For example, following recent outages in Microsoft services and a technical glitch in the U.S. air traffic control system, some interpreted these as signs of an impending digital apocalypse. There's even a date — November 17th. The theory goes that hackers will break into the world's biggest banks, wipe out everyone's accounts, and shut down the internet for three months, sending the world into chaos and panic. Such fears could also spill over into financial markets, affecting investor confidence and driving demand for safe-haven assets, while putting the U.S. dollar index in focus. The good news is that there's no master switch to turn off the internet. It's a huge network of undersea cables, satellites, data centers, and telecom operators, so taking the whole thing offline is unlikely. Still, the global network does face real threats, just not the kind these theories suggest. A much more likely scenario is a major outage caused by shared dependencies, when multiple services suddenly lose access to the same cloud provider. And we have seen this happen more than once in recent years.

title: Kuroda, once Japan's great easer, says BOJ rates may need to rise above neutral
body: For Japanese rates and the yen, a call for above-neutral rates from the architect of Japan's easing era adds weight to the hawkish tail of BOJ pricing. Most economists see a terminal rate near 1.75%, and talk of 2.5% now has a high-profile backer. Kuroda no longer sets policy, so the direct effect is limited. Still, his critique of the food tax cut puts the fiscal-monetary tension in sharp relief ahead of an expected December hike. Front-end JGB yields, with the two-year near 1.88%, are most exposed to any shift toward a higher peak. Oil matters here too. Kuroda explicitly links Japan's inflation risk to the Iran war, so a renewed energy spike would strengthen the case he describes. --- The governor who took Japan into negative rates now says the BOJ may need to go beyond neutral. He blames imported inflation from the Iran war and a food tax cut he says will feed prices, not growth. Summary: Former BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda says rates may need to rise above neutral if inflation becomes more serious. He cited cost pressures from the US war with Iran, given Japan's reliance on imported oil, materials and food. The BOJ is widely expected to hike next month. Economists see a peak of 1.75%, and some see as high as 2.5%. Kuroda said PM Takaichi's planned food sales tax cut, worth about ¥10 trillion, would push up prices, not growth. He described Japan's July to September contraction as probably temporary.

title: Why Warren Buffet and Berkshire Hathaway keep going back to airlines
body: Berkshire Hathaway is buying more Delta Air Lines and I think there's a fascinating story behind why Warren Buffett and his successors keep getting drawn back into the airline business. Berkshire's latest 13F filing, released late Monday, showed it increased its stake in Delta by 7.13 million shares in the third quarter, or 12.4%, bringing its total holdings to 64.45 million shares, or nearly 10% of the company. That's the third consecutive quarter Berkshire has built its position. It started with 39.8 million shares at the end of March, increased that to 57.3 million in June and has now added another 7.1 million. This isn't a small position anymore, and the steady accumulation suggests growing conviction even as the war in Iran and fuel price spike have hurt airline economics. What's particularly interesting is Berkshire's long and tortured history with airlines. Buffett famously described himself as an "aeroholic" and joked about having a telephone hotline to stop him from buying airline stocks. He also repeated the old joke that the fastest way to become a millionaire was to start as a billionaire and buy an airline. In his 2007 shareholder letter, he described airlines as the worst kind of business: one that grows rapidly, requires enormous amounts of capital and ultimately earns little or nothing. Yet Berkshire keeps buying them.

title: US Sept business inventories +0.5% vs +0.4% prior
body: Prior was +0.4% Retail inventories ex-autos +0.5% vs +0.4% prior This report is rarely a market mover but it's an input into GDP, so a strong number will boost tracking estimates and vice versa. For background, the Census Bureau's Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales report, known as business inventories, is released monthly at 10 am ET about six weeks after the reference month ends. It combines inventories and sales across the three main stages of the goods supply chain: manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers. Much of the report is known by the time it's released. Manufacturing inventories come out in the factory orders report, and advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories are published about two weeks earlier in the Advance Economic Indicators release. Business inventories adds the full retail figures and pulls everything into a combined total, so the headline change in total business inventories rarely surprises. Retail inventories are the most useful piece. They're broken down by type of store, including motor vehicle and parts dealers, general merchandise, food and beverage stores, clothing, furniture and building materials. Auto dealer inventories swing sharply with production schedules, supply disruptions and incentives, so economists focus on retail inventories excluding autos. That measure feeds directly into the inventory investment component of GDP and often prompts revisions to growth estimates.

title: Home Depot earnings offer a mixed picture of the US consumer as spending improves but traffic remains weak
body: Home Depot reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and sales on Tuesday but shares fell 1.9% in premarket trading as the company faces margin pressure. It's the first of the major retailers to report this week. The home improvement giant reported adjusted earnings of $3.86 per share compared to $3.84 expected, while revenue of $43.4 billion topped the $42.8 billion consensus. The more interesting numbers are buried deeper in the report and offer some clues about the health of the US consumer. Comparable sales rose 2.2% in the quarter, including a matching 2.2% increase in the US. That's an improvement from the 0.2% growth reported a year ago and suggests some stabilization in home improvement spending. However, the composition of that growth is telling. Comparable sales: +2.2% Comparable customer transactions: -0.5% Comparable average ticket: +3.0% Average ticket: $93.09 versus $90.39 a year ago In other words, customers are spending more when they visit Home Depot, but they're still visiting and buying less frequently. It looks more like inflation than a healthy consumer but there is some sequential improvement here. Transactions fell 1.6% in the same quarter last year, so the pace of decline has moderated considerably. Still, the recovery in spending is being driven by larger tickets rather than more transactions.

title: NAHB housing market index for November 25 vs 29 estimate

It measures the real output of the US industrial sector and is one of the few major economic reports produced by the Fed itself. The headline industrial production index covers three sectors: manufacturing, which accounts for roughly three-quarters of the total, mining and utilities.

title: Riddle: Buyers were more aggressive, yet stock prices fell. How is that possible?
body: When financial commentators say buyers were more aggressive than sellers, what exactly do they mean? And if every trade has a buyer and a seller, how can there be more buying than selling? Let's solve a market riddle that explains how trading really works. Imagine reading a financial article that says: "Buyers were more aggressive than sellers, yet prices continued to fall." Wait a minute. Doesn't that sound contradictory? If buyers are more aggressive, shouldn't prices go up? And what does "aggressive buying" even mean? Are people buying more shares? Are wealthy investors spending more money? Are there more buyers than sellers? The answer is surprisingly interesting, and understanding it can change how you think about financial markets. You don't need to be a professional trader, understand complicated charts or even own a single share to follow along. Let's start with the basics. First, what does it mean to be an aggressive buyer? Imagine you want to buy one share of a company. You check its price and discover something interesting. There isn't really just one price. There are two prices that matter when you're about to trade. $99.95 is the bid. That's the highest price someone is currently offering to pay for a share. $100.00 is the ask. That's the lowest price someone is currently offering to accept for a share. The difference between those prices, five cents, is called the spread. Now you have two choices.

title: Fed's Williams: The economy is getting stronger, inflation not moving in the right direction
body: New York Fed President John Williams is out with some fresh commentary, and the message is a classic mix of acknowledging the inflation headache while trying to keep the market from pricing in anything too aggressive. I don't think the situation calls for dramatic policy action Tariffs and energy shock still affecting inflation readings Is seeing signs of shocks spilling over into broader inflation data Inflation is 'stubbornly high' Fed still has more work to do to get inflation back to 2% The economy is strong and getting stronger, inflation is not moving in right direction The big takeaway here for traders is that line about avoiding "dramatic policy action." Coming off the back of this week's hot October CPI print—and with the market increasingly jittery about the Fed having to ramp up its hiking cycle after restarting it in September—Williams is effectively pouring cold water on the idea of a 50 bps move. Still, you can't ignore the hawkish undertones. Admitting that tariff and energy shocks are spilling over into the broader data is a notable shift. Back in October, Williams was singing a much more patient tune, arguing there was "no need for urgency" ahead of the late-October FOMC meeting and suggesting he saw no need for hikes in 2027. While he was open to one more quarter-point hike before year-end back then, the tone today is noticeably more concerned about the stickiness of prices—even if he isn't ready to panic.
